newsitem.title: NORWAY: Statoil posts record '96 operating profit.
newsitem.headline: Statoil posts record '96 operating profit.

text.p: State Norwegian oil company Den norske stats oljeselskap AS (Statoil) said on Thursday it achieved record operating profits in 1996 thanks to higher crude prices, increased production and stable operations.
The company posted operating profits of 18.2 billion crowns ($2.7 billion), a rise of 34 percent from 13.6 billion crowns in 1995. However, net profits were steady at 5.3 billion crowns.

Statoil said the steady after-tax figure was because a significant share of revenues came from offshore operations -- which attract far higher tax than land-based activities -- while less-taxed petrochemicals showed a decline in earnings.

"The 1996 result is good and Statoil's financial position has been strengthened," Harald Norvik, Statoil chief executive, said in a statement. "An operating profit of NOK 18.2 billion is an important step towards our target of NOK 25 billion in operating profit by 2000."

Operating profits for exploration and production rose 4.5 billion crowns to 16.8 billion crowns, reflecting higher output and an average oil price of 133 crowns per barrel in 1996 compared with 108 crowns per barrel a year earlier.
"The market was on our side in 1996," Norvik said in the statement. Later he told a news conference he expected prices to fall.
"We must be prepared for lower oil prices now than we had in 1996. Our investments are naturally based on oil prices that are considerably lower than the ones we see at present," he said.

Earnings from refining and marketing improved more than fourfold to 1.7 billion crowns from 400 million crowns, while petrochemicals tumbled to 200 million crowns from a record year in 1995 at 1.1 billion.
Statoil attributed the slump to a drop in prices for plastic raw materials. The company's main activity in this area is its 50-50 Borealis joint venture with Finland's Neste Oy.

Equity crude production averaged 464,000 barrels per day (bpd), up from 424,000 bpd in 1995, while international oil and gas production rose to 30,000 barrels of oil equivalent (boe) per day from 12,000 boe per day.
Statoil said commercial oil reserves increased 2.5 percent to 1.899 billion barrels from 1.853 billion barrels, while gas reserves climbed to 337 billion cubic metres from 324 billion cubic metres.

"The basis for Statoil as an energy company is the availability of oil and gas reserves. I am very happy that we have managed to increase our reserves despite the high production we've had," Norvik told reporters.
"Our target is an oil production of 500,000 barrels per day at Statoil's fields on the Norwegian (continental) shelf in the year 2000, and to keep that level until 2005. We believe we can do that."

Statoil said efforts to improve oil recovery and cut production costs at the giant North Sea Statfjord complex had yielded substantial gains. Operating costs on its fields and pipeline systems fell nine percent from 1995 to 1996.
Norvik said the recovery factor at Statfjord was planned at around 70 percent and the company aimed to improve the recovery rate at Heidrun from 28 percent to 50 percent.
